articles.summary: Measles cases in Japan rose to 197 (preliminary) by March 29, the highest for this point since the COVID-19 era, up from 60 last year. The JiHS (National Institute of Health Crisis Management) reported 30 new cases in the week ending March 29. Tokyo leads with 48 cases, Kagoshima 24, including a Kagoshima City high school graduation ceremony cluster. The surge is attributed to overseas-imported viruses spreading domestically. There is no antiviral treatment; vaccination is preventive. Japan’s routine two-dose vaccination is publicly funded: first dose at age 1 and a second before entering school; private vaccination is also available. About 70% of patients had one dose or an unknown vaccination history. JiHS urges checking vaccination status, especially for travelers, healthcare workers, and foreign visitors, to curb ongoing transmission.

articles.summary: Measles infections in Japan total 152 cases nationwide through March 22, 2026, the highest since 2020. The highly contagious measles virus causes illness about 10 days after exposure, with high fever (≥39°C) and rash, and can lead to encephalitis. Japan was certified measles eliminated by the World Health Organization in 2015, but since 2023, outbreaks abroad have seeded domestic transmission through returnees and inbound travelers. Health Minister Ken'ichirō Ueno urged that anyone with suspected symptoms should avoid public transportation and seek medical care promptly; those in the target age group for routine vaccination or with uncertain vaccination history are advised to consider vaccination. The report emphasizes vigilance against imported cases fueling local spread and underscores ongoing public health measures.

articles.headlineTranslated: Measles infections on the rise; we must not underestimate them and must prevent their spread.
articles.summary: Measles infections are rising in Japan, with 152 cases nationwide by March 22 this year—the second-fastest pace since 2019. Tokyo reports the highest numbers, already surpassing last year’s total, while Aichi prefecture notes a high school cluster. Other notable activity occurs in major urban areas such as Chiba, Kanagawa, Saitama, and Osaka. The surge is attributed to international importations from returning travelers and inbound visitors. Despite 2015 WHO elimination status, global outbreaks have led some countries to lose elimination designation. Measles spreads by contact, droplets, and airborne routes; unimmunized individuals can contract it simply by sharing a room with an infectious person. When cases are detected, rapid exposure notification is encouraged to minimize secondary spread. There is no antiviral treatment; vaccination prevents infection. Japan’s routine schedule provides two doses for those born since 2000 (at 1 year and before school entry). Those never infected or unvaccinated are at higher risk; antibody testing is available. Severe measles can cause encephalitis in about 1 in 1,000 infections.

Early symptoms resemble a cold (fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctival injection), but a high fever (>39°C) with a generalized rash and Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa typically follow, sometimes with a two-peak fever. If suspected, contact a clinic by phone before visiting; wear a mask and avoid public transport. Vaccination, ideally two doses, is the strongest defense; incomplete vaccination should be followed with antibody testing or boosters. Complications include pneumonia, otitis media, encephalitis (~1 in 1000 deaths) and rare SSPE years later.

Dr. Hideki Kawamura of Kagoshima University warns the rise is linked to more overseas travelers and inbound visitors introducing the virus. Measles is highly contagious and can be transmitted by sharing air. Early symptoms include fever, cough, conjunctival injection, followed by rash and white oral spots (Koplik spots); infants risk pneumonia, teens risk encephalitis. Although WHO declared measles eliminated in 2015, outbreaks persist in Southeast Asia, and the U.S. outbreak last year contributed. Vaccination is critical: routine is two doses at age 1 and before entering elementary school. Born Oct 2, 1972–Apr 1, 1990: one dose; earlier births may be unvaccinated but may have immunity. Kawamura urges verifying vaccination history—via the mother-child health handbook—before international travel.

Authorities are advising through schools and publicly sharing exposure histories when large public contact occurred.

articles.summary: Measles is spreading nationwide in Japan, with over 100 confirmed cases in 2026 as of March 24, 2026, prompting spring-break travel warnings. While Yamanashi Prefecture has seen no cases since 2019, the national outbreak continues, with case counts this year approaching half of last year's total. Measles is spread by airborne transmission; early symptoms include cough, high fever, and red eyes, followed by a full-body red rash 3–4 days after onset. There is no specific antiviral treatment; complications can be fatal. Dr. Hiroshi Akaba, pediatrics at Yamanashi University Hospital, notes rising infections worldwide, especially in the United States and Southeast Asia, making travel returnees higher risk. Emphasis on vaccination as the primary preventive measure; due to airborne spread, standard handwashing and masks may be insufficient. If red rash or suspected exposure occurs, consult a healthcare facility by phone before visiting.

articles.headlineTranslated: Explainer: Measles cases have surged 40-fold in three years — How to prevent it? Airborne transmission is also possible at ten times the strength of influenza (Posted March 24, 2026) | YTV NEWS NNN
articles.summary: Measles cases have surged about 40-fold over three years, with airborne transmission driving spread. Measles is highly contagious, about three times more infectious than COVID-19 and more than ten times that of influenza. Symptoms include fever, cough, and runny nose, followed by a rash after fever peaks; immune suppression can raise the risk of complications, with a case fatality rate around 0.1%. The virus propagates via tiny airborne particles, allowing spread in indoor settings. A notable 2016 incident at Kansai International Airport, Japan, involved an imported source and produced a cluster of 33 staff members. To curb transmission, locations used by measles patients have been publicly disclosed to aid containment. The message emphasizes awareness of airborne spread and rapid response to suspected cases to prevent further import/export-linked outbreaks.

articles.summary: Measles outbreak in Japan reaches 139 confirmed cases this year, up from 32 at the same point last year—more than fourfold. Tokyo accounts for the largest share with 32 cases, followed by Aichi Prefecture with 23 and Chiba Prefecture with 16. Measles is highly contagious; in susceptible individuals infection nearly always develops. Common symptoms include fever above 39°C and rash, with possible complications such as pneumonia and otitis media. The MHLW urged those with suspected symptoms to contact medical facilities by phone in advance and to avoid using public transportation when traveling, highlighting the need for vaccination and public health precautions to curb transmission.

articles.headlineTranslated: Editorial: Measles on the Rise; Ensure Thorough Two-Dose Vaccination
articles.summary: Measles cases in Japan totalled 100 from January 1 to March 8, 2026, far exceeding 22 in the same period last year and the decade-high since 2019. Measles is airborne with about a 10-day incubation; symptoms include fever, cough, conjunctivitis, and rash, with pneumonia or encephalitis possible and rare post-infectious encephalitis years later. Control hinges on the MR vaccine (measles-rubella) given twice: at age 1 and before elementary school. About 70% of current patients are aged 10–30, many have not completed two doses. Latest vaccination rates: first dose 92.7%, second dose 91.0%, below the 95% target. Declines in vaccination also appear in the US, UK, and Canada, linked to hesitancy; UK/Canada recently lost WHO elimination status. Japan remains an elimination country, but domestic transmission could jeopardize that status. Cases are imported via travel.

articles.summary: Measles infections are rising domestically in Japan. From January 2026 through March 8, 2026, the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare reports about 100 infections—the highest for the period since the COVID-19 era. Virus analyses indicate most cases are imported, linked to returning travelers and inbound visitors to Japan. Although vaccination coverage against measles is high among Japanese, some age groups remain unvaccinated or have no prior infection, creating pockets of susceptibility. Experts say the immediate risk of a large nationwide outbreak is low, but continued vigilance is needed as imported cases could sustain transmission. Emphasis on vaccination and robust surveillance is essential to prevent expansion of domestic spread from imported sources.

articles.headlineTranslated: I thought it was hay fever... Measles, of all things. Early symptoms closely resembled hay fever; dangerous self-diagnosis. Doctors warn.
articles.summary: Measles outbreaks in Japan are driven by imported cases and the virus’s high transmissibility. Nationwide reports rose through early 2025, with 119 measles patients from January to mid-May, median age 24; 20s accounted for 34%, followed by 30s–40s; 79% had incomplete or unknown two-dose vaccination histories. A February Tokyo Dome concert attendee was diagnosed with modified measles, underscoring adult vulnerability. Guidance from clinicians in Kanagawa Prefecture (Sagamihara) emphasizes measles’ airborne, droplet, and contact transmission; infectiousness can persist after the patient leaves spaces like airports, trains, event venues, shopping centers, and medical facilities. Incubation is about 10–12 days, with fever, cough, runny nose, and red eyes; early symptoms can resemble hay fever, risking delayed diagnosis. Ongoing outbreaks stem from resumed international travel, overseas measles activity, and prior WHO elimination in 2015; vaccination remains the primary prevention strategy.

articles.summary: Measles cases surge in Japan, with 87 infections reported through March 4, 2026, far above 9 at the same point last year. Tokyo Metropolis and Aichi Prefecture are among affected areas; officials warn many cases are imported from overseas, with about 15 infections (roughly 17%) presumed acquired abroad, notably in Indonesia and other Southeast Asian countries. Japan remains in a measles-elimination status, suggesting additional domestic cases are likely imported. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare has issued notices to prefectures to alert travelers and encourage reporting of travel history, urging preventive vaccination for those traveling to outbreak regions or in contact with vulnerable individuals. Measles is highly contagious; basic measures may be insufficient. Emphasized is routine vaccination at ages 1 and 5–6, and adults should verify vaccination history before travel or exposure. Dr. Nobuhiko Okabe of Kawasaki City Health Safety Research Institute warns of rapid spread and the need to prevent domestic re-establishment.

articles.headlineTranslated: Measles cases reported in succession: a teenage male in Kagoshima City and a woman in her 40s from outside the prefecture.
articles.summary: As of March 10, 2026, Kagoshima Prefecture and Kagoshima City confirmed two measles cases: a teenage male in Kagoshima City and a woman in her 40s from outside the prefecture. Both were exposed to multiples during the infectious period. The teen’s laboratory-confirmed infection (reported March 9) is linked to a prior case confirmed February 6; between February 28 and March 6 he attended a skills test and visited commercial facilities in the city. The woman’s infection is an imported case with overseas travel during the incubation period; she entered the prefecture on March 7 by a friend’s car and was reported March 9, with no use of public transit or local facilities. Public Health authorities urge medical consultation if measles is suspected and to pursue vaccination; the prefecture indicates two to three measles cases have been confirmed in 2026 so far.

articles.headlineTranslated: Measles cases in Tokyo reach 12 so far this year... Tokyo Medical Association calls for vaccination, "Herd immunity is declining."
articles.summary: Measles cases in Tokyo reach 12 by early March 2026, prompting the Tokyo Medical Association to emphasize vaccination as herd immunity declines. Tokyo’s measles counts have varied over the past decade, with a 2019 peak of 124 cases, zero cases in 2021–22 during the COVID-19 period, then 34 in the previous year, and 12 by early March 2026, a pace well above 2025. The virus causes fever, cough, and runny nose after about a 10-day incubation, followed by fever above 39°C and a rash; it spreads via airborne, droplet, and contact transmission, with about 1 in 1,000 infections fatal. Vaccination markedly lowers infection risk. Notably, several cases involved exposure to many people in major hospitals and other public facilities. Doctors urge those with suspected measles to contact clinics before visiting and to separate suspected patients in care settings.

articles.summary: Measles outbreak in Kagoshima Prefecture: The third case of the year confirmed in a woman in her 40s who lives outside the prefecture. She traveled on March 6 from Shiojiri Station, Nagano Prefecture, by JR to Hakata Station, then by a friend's car to Kagoshima. Fever began March 7; rash appeared March 8. She visited Kawaso Public Health Center facility on March 8, and genotype testing confirmed infection on March 9. The prefecture urges anyone who used the same transport during the same time frame to seek medical care if fever or rash develops within 21 days. Measles is highly contagious via droplets or contact. Earlier in March, measles was confirmed in Kagoshima City, and a teenage male case was reported on March 9 as part of the ongoing outbreak.
